svg.aria-label: Three routes for a call to a chiropractic office. Route one, book it: new patient requests, reschedules, hours, directions, forms, and insurance questions that are answered from a written sheet. Route two, flag for the doctor: recent accident or fall, numbness or weakness, pain that is getting rapidly worse, a new severe headache with neck pain, fever with back pain, or a patient who feels worse after an adjustment; the script captures the caller's words, does not book a routine slot and notifies the chiropractor. Route three, 911 now: stroke signs, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness in the groin or saddle area, weakness in both legs, or chest pain; the script tells the caller to call 911 and then notifies the chiropractor. The script never decides between routes two and three by asking clinical questions of its own.
svg.text: Every call goes through one of three doors
The script's only clinical skill is recognising which door. The list behind doors two and three is written and signed by the chiropractor.

g.text: New patient wants a first visit
Intake forms and what to bring

svg.text: answered only from your written sheet
no routine slot until a clinician decides

g.text: New severe headache with neck pain
Fever or feeling unwell with back pain

svg.text: Caller's own words captured, doctor notified

g.text: Loss of bladder or bowel control
Numbness in the groin or saddle area

svg.text: Emergency services first, then the doctor
Ask follow-up clinical questions to choose between doors two and three. If the caller's words are on either list, it takes the more cautious door.
Symptom lists adapted from the AANS, the NHS and the CDC - see sources. An illustration, not a clinical protocol: your chiropractor writes the real one.
